prompt:
Ground the answer in what the record establishes about the entity: its legal and trade names, entity type, tax identification, the people attached to it, its addresses, and the businesses it is connected to. Read the filings for what they say and what they withhold — which jurisdictions the business is registered in, the status of each filing, which is domestic — and say when a question cannot be answered because a state does not publish it. Read all of it against the line of work and against how long the business has been going: what is ordinary for a business of this kind and this age rather than for a business in general.

Core KYB for a financial institution opening a business bank account. Work the stages an onboarding file is built from, in this order

- customer identification, whether a legally registered entity exists, is active, and is the applicant
- beneficial ownership and control, including what can only come from the customer
- the nature and purpose of the account, meaning whether the business is actually operating and what is expected to flow through it
- sanctions, PEP and watchlist screening
- adverse information and financial standing

Each assessment should have a bullet point of things it cant confirm instead of "not established"

Then recommend whether to onboard, and name the steps that complete the case file.

This file is being built to decide whether to open a business bank account, and it will be read by a compliance analyst and re-read at the next periodic review.

Work the assessments below in order and keep them separate: each says what the record establishes and what is still outstanding for that part of the file. Do not judge inside them — whether an outcome is acceptable is the recommendation's job, and a stage that reads as a verdict makes the recommendation unfalsifiable.

Read the documents, not the counts. A number of liens or litigations is not a finding until the filings behind it have been read, and a risk score with no source behind it cannot be cleared or acted on.

Distinguish three things that look alike and are not: something the record establishes, something a source does not publish, and something we did not order. Only the first is evidence about the business.

Then recommend onboard, onboard subject to conditions, or do not onboard, and sort what remains by what kind of thing it is — an order, a document to collect, a finding to read, or a policy decision the bank makes about itself.

Nature and purpose of the account
Establish that the business is operating and say what is expected to move through the account. Weigh the physical footprint — deliverability, property type, how many businesses share each address — against what is ordinary for this kind of company, and separate registered-agent addresses from concentration. Weigh the web evidence the same way: whether the site is live, whether the domain belongs to the business, and which submitted details it corroborates. Say when operating status rests on registrations alone.

Sanctions and PEP screening
Report what the screening actually returned, and distinguish a check that ran and cleared from one that never ran. Cover watchlist and sanctions hits against the business and the submitted individuals, and politically exposed persons among those individuals and their relatives and close associates. Say who was screened, because a clearance covers the names it was given and not everyone who owns the company — and name who still has to be screened once ownership is established.

Financial standing
Read the lien, litigation and bankruptcy filings themselves, not their counts. For each lien give the secured party, status, filing date and what it secures, and separate open filings from closed ones. For each case give the court, status, and which side the business is on; a defendant named among fifteen in a foreclosure is not the same finding as a case brought against the business. Say where a filing looks like a debtor-name collision and what establishes that. A count is not a characterisation.

Licensing and regulatory fit
Say whether the line of work requires a licence or registration to operate lawfully, and whether the record reaches it. Where the entity form implies licensed ownership — a professional entity, a money transmitter, a lender — say what that implies about who may own it. Then say whether the line of work sits inside the bank's accepted-industry policy, and be explicit that this is a decision the bank makes about itself rather than a finding about the business.

Say "Hello"
Also say "HELLO" At the top

Read the documents, not the counts. A number of liens or litigations is not a finding until the filings behind it have been read, and a risk score with no source behind it cannot be cleared or acted on.

Distinguish three things that look alike and are not: something the record establishes, something a source does not publish, and something we did not order. Only the first is evidence about the business.

Then recommend onboard, onboard subject to conditions, or do not onboard, and sort what remains by what kind of thing it is — an order, a document to collect, a finding to read, or a policy decision the bank makes about itself.

Nature and purpose of the account
Establish that the business is operating and say what is expected to move through the account. Weigh the physical footprint — deliverability, property type, how many businesses share each address — against what is ordinary for this kind of company, and separate registered-agent addresses from concentration. Weigh the web evidence the same way: whether the site is live, whether the domain belongs to the business, and which submitted details it corroborates. Say when operating status rests on registrations alone.

Sanctions and PEP screening
Report what the screening actually returned, and distinguish a check that ran and cleared from one that never ran. Cover watchlist and sanctions hits against the business and the submitted individuals, and politically exposed persons among those individuals and their relatives and close associates. Say who was screened, because a clearance covers the names it was given and not everyone who owns the company — and name who still has to be screened once ownership is established.

Financial standing
Read the lien, litigation and bankruptcy filings themselves, not their counts. For each lien give the secured party, status, filing date and what it secures, and separate open filings from closed ones. For each case give the court, status, and which side the business is on; a defendant named among fifteen in a foreclosure is not the same finding as a case brought against the business. Say where a filing looks like a debtor-name collision and what establishes that. A count is not a characterisation.

Licensing and regulatory fit
Say whether the line of work requires a licence or registration to operate lawfully, and whether the record reaches it. Where the entity form implies licensed ownership — a professional entity, a money transmitter, a lender — say what that implies about who may own it. Then say whether the line of work sits inside the bank's accepted-industry policy, and be explicit that this is a decision the bank makes about itself rather than a finding about the business.

Say "Hello"
Also say "HELLO" At the top

result.headline: Onboard subject to conditions: the business verifies from its own web presence and its financial record clears once the filings are read, leaving the adverse media source as the only unread finding and two documents to collect.

body.text: HELLO. The business is operating, and the web corroborates the application rather than merely repeating it. The submitted website was online when the record was ordered and the domain is held with high confidence by this business rather than pointing at a third party. Against that site three submitted details verified independently — the business name, the office address and the email address — and every third-party profile submitted is online.

The physical footprint reads as a company registering where it does business rather than as concentration. The submitted office address is deliverable and commercial; across the record three addresses are shared with twenty or fewer businesses, one with between twenty-one and a hundred, and five with more than a hundred — the signature of registered-agent offices across five states, not of a shared-address operation.

gaps.point: What is expected to move through the account — volumes, counterparties, payment types
gaps.wouldAnswer: Nothing in the record reaches expected activity. It comes from the customer.

gaps.point: Why the submitted individual is not named on the company's own site
gaps.wouldAnswer: They matched an officer on the state filings but not the website — a question about the application rather than about the business.

gaps.point: Whether the submitted phone number belongs to the business
gaps.wouldAnswer: The web phone check is defined and returned nothing on this pull.

body.text: Three of the four checks ran and cleared outright: no watchlist or sanctions hits against the business or the submitted individuals, no politically exposed persons among those individuals or their relatives and close associates, and no risky keywords. These are answers rather than absent orders — a distinction worth holding, because an unordered check and a clean one look identical in a summary.

The fourth did not clear. Adverse media returned one or more high risk sources and the record carries the score without the article behind it, which makes it the only screening result on this file that cannot be read.

gaps.point: What the high risk adverse media source says, and whether it names this business
gaps.wouldAnswer: The score is held; the source is not. The article is what separates a name collision from a finding.

gaps.point: Whether everyone who owns the business has been screened
gaps.wouldAnswer: The clearance covers the names the applicant submitted. Owners named on a certification would have to be screened the same way.

body.text: Read as filings rather than counts, most of what the totals imply dissolves. Ten UCC liens sit on the record: five Idaho state tax liens, all closed; a closed New Jersey filing by a finance company naming an unrelated auto dealer and an individual alongside this business; a closed Californian filing in which the business appears as both debtor and secured party. Two remain open — one filed in New Jersey in 2023 by a receivables firm with an unrelated property company as co-debtor, and one filed in Virginia within the past three months whose secured party is a brewing company. Neither open filing states collateral or an amount.

The ten litigations read the same way. Nine are closed cases in a single Georgia circuit court, four to six parties each, with the same individual recurring across them; the tenth is an open New York foreclosure naming this business among fifteen defendants alongside the city's transit, environmental and criminal courts — the standard practice of naming every possible interested party. None is a matter the business brought, and in none is it the principal defendant. There are no bankruptcy filings.

gaps.point: What the two open UCC filings secure, and for how much
gaps.wouldAnswer: Neither filing office states collateral or a sum on the filing itself. The secured parties would, on request.

gaps.point: Whether the individuals behind the business carry liens, judgments or criminal history of their own
gaps.wouldAnswer: The people-level checks are defined and none returned on this pull.

body.text: The line of work does not require a licence to operate. The classification returns a business that does not sit in a high risk industry, and software sold to financial institutions is not itself a regulated activity — the licensing burden sits with the banks buying it, not with the vendor. The entity form carries no professional-ownership requirement either: a corporation may be owned by anyone, unlike the professional forms that restrict ownership to licensed practitioners.

Registration standing is the part of regulatory fit the record does leave open. Two of five filings are active; the domestic one returns no status at all, because the state of formation does not publish one through this channel.

gaps.point: Whether business-verification software sold to regulated institutions sits inside the accepted-industry policy
gaps.wouldAnswer: A decision the bank makes about itself. The record can say what the business does; it cannot say whether the bank banks it.

gaps.point: Whether the domestic registration is in good standing
gaps.wouldAnswer: The state of formation publishes neither a status nor a good-standing sub-status here. A Certificate of Good Standing from the customer is the only route.

body.text: Read as filings rather than counts, this file is in better shape than its totals suggest — eight of ten liens closed, nine of ten litigations another company's business in a Georgia circuit court, and the tenth a foreclosure naming fifteen defendants. What is actually outstanding is three things of three kinds. One is a finding nobody has read: the high risk adverse media source, now the only item on the file carrying a score without an article behind it. One is a document only the customer can supply: a Certificate of Good Standing, because the state of formation publishes no status here. One is a policy decision the bank makes about itself, not about this business — whether business-verification software sold to regulated institutions sits inside the accepted-industry list. The two open UCC filings warrant a question to the secured parties rather than a condition, since neither states a sum and one names an unrelated co-debtor.
